claims.statement: MovieCollectionManager's core components are mcm-app (universal Expo/React Native frontend fronted by the BFF), mc-service (Rust/Axum service owning all movie-collection domain logic and the sole writer to mc-db), mc-db (a single shared MongoDB database mc_db with movie_collections and movies collections), and Keycloak as the external IAM provider expecting a movie-collection-manager client with mc-admin/mc-user client roles (new self-registrations default to mc-user).

Access control in MCM is split into two independent layers: RBAC (Keycloak client roles mc-admin vs mc-user, enforced before a request reaches domain logic) and DAC (per-collection owner/contributor/viewer rights recorded in each collection's own acl array in movie_collections, enforced inside mc-service, with no notion of individual collections at the Keycloak layer).

Feature 073 adds a per-user scheduled/on-demand backup capability run in-process by the BFF: it copies a user's own collections to an S3-compatible or WebDAV destination the user owns and supplies, retains the last N versions, and restores only by creating new collections (never overwriting live data); unattended runs authenticate via a Keycloak offline token the user explicitly consented to, and destination secrets are sealed under their own encryption key (BACKUP_CREDENTIAL_ENC_KEY), separate from the agent-config encryption key (AGENT_CONFIG_ENC_KEY). This is a BFF-owned capability, not part of mc-service or mc-db.

Grant/revoke of contributor/viewer DAC rights is not yet built in the product: mc-service authorizes against the acl array and tests populate non-owner roles, but no UI or endpoint exists to actually grant or revoke a contributor/viewer entry, so every real collection's acl today contains only the owner entry.

The AI Agents layer (Agent Gateway, movie-mcp, movie-assistant) is additive: mc-service and existing mcm-app screens are unchanged, and every agent-originated call to mc-service is routed through movie-mcp carrying a downscoped, audience-bound user token, so the existing RBAC (mc-admin/mc-user) and DAC (owner/contributor/viewer) enforcement applies unchanged rather than being bypassed.

mc-db must run as a single-member replica set (mongod --replSet rs0, initialised by rs-init, with mc-service connecting via directConnection=true) rather than a plain standalone mongod, because collection_repository.rs's atomic cascade-delete relies on a MongoDB multi-document transaction that only a replica-set-enabled deployment can start.

The dev mc-db compose service carries two dev-only resource tunings. `--wiredTigerCacheSizeGB 1` caps a WiredTiger cache whose default is roughly half of host RAM, and `--setParameter wiredTigerFileHandleCloseIdleTime=30 --setParameter wiredTigerFileHandleCloseMinimum=250` restore WiredTiger's own sweeper thresholds in place of MongoDB's raised pair (`closeIdleTime=600 s`, `closeMinimum=2000`). Without the sweeper pair, the integration harness's per-test database churn left 65,844 WiredTiger data handles open for 2 live collections, nothing was ever eligible for sweeping, and mongod was OOM-killed mid-run, surfacing as "unexpected end of file" / connection-refused / server-selection-timeout errors indistinguishable from a MongoDB consistency bug (item #468). Both flags are startup-only (`setParameter` is refused at runtime) and neither reaches production, where `compose.prod.yaml` carries its own `mongod` command.

The BFF owns its own MongoDB instance (`mcm-bff-db`, holding per-user agent config) that is physically separate from mc-service's `mc-db`, because no component reaches across a service boundary into another service's database; `mcm-bff-db` is a plain standalone `mongod` with no replica set and no directConnection because the BFF does single-document upserts only, unlike `mc-db` whose single-member replica set exists for mc-service's cascade-delete transaction.

mc-service runs Keycloak OIDC discovery and the JWKS fetch in a background task at startup, so it binds and serves immediately even when Keycloak is unreachable: /health still answers but every protected request is rejected with 401. A *failed* discovery still marks the auth instance ready, so integration tests must gate on discovery actually succeeding (is_operational) rather than on the attempt completing, otherwise the whole auth-negative suite passes green against a dead Keycloak.

Feature 073's backup destination containers live in their own compose file (`infrastructure-as-code/docker/backups/compose.yaml`) rather than a profile inside the `mcm` stack, because the `mcm` stack is one Compose project whose `include:` pulls in every component file and Compose interpolates every service of an included file at parse time regardless of which profiles are selected — so a required `${REGISTRY_HOST:?}` inside a profile-gated service aborted `up` for the whole stack, including CI's app-e2e bring-up which wants none of those services. Feature 080 removed the offending from-source object-store image (the S3 oracle is now upstream RustFS pinned by digest), so the variable is gone and CI's bring-up step passes no registry input, but the separate file remains because a profile is not isolation from interpolation.

The BFF's backup scheduler is an in-process `setInterval` in `server.js` that POSTs to `/bff-api/backups/tick` over 127.0.0.1 with the tick secret, is disabled outright (announced once at boot) when `BACKUP_TICK_SECRET` is unset, logs only when a job actually ran, and never fires under `pnpm start` because `server.js` does not run under Metro — in dev the tick route must be called directly.

The Agent Gateway and its `agent-db` checkpoint store are private-network only and the client never reaches them: only the BFF starts a run (over an AG-UI stream, attaching a run-scoped delegation token as a non-checkpointed value), and the gateway's single shared in-process MCP client re-exchanges that token per identity-bearing tool call, so each `movie-mcp` call carries a downscoped, short-TTL, audience-bound token that mc-service validates exactly like a human request.

The backup-destinations compose file is standalone: it attaches to the `mcm` stack's `mcm-bff-network` as an `external` network (so `up` fails when the `mcm` stack is not already running, which is the correct answer since the BFF is what writes there), and because it is a separate file in the same Compose project the stack's own `down` does not reach it — teardown requires a second `docker compose -f infrastructure-as-code/docker/backups/compose.yaml down`, or the persistent CI runner silently reuses the previous run's destinations.

Both backup destination servers bind only to `127.0.0.1`, and they are reachable by the BFF in dev/CI only because the environment generators seed their hostnames into `BACKUP_ALLOWED_DESTINATION_HOSTS` — the BFF's backup-destination URL guard denies loopback/private/link-local space by default (the inverse of the Ollama guard, which expects a LAN endpoint), so an allow-list entry is the guard working rather than a misconfiguration to route around.

The feature-073 backup destinations are REAL servers rather than hand-written fixtures — an S3-compatible object store (upstream RustFS, pulled by digest) and Apache httpd serving WebDAV via `mod_dav` — because the S3 and WebDAV drivers are tested in the integration tier precisely so the dialect they are tested against is a real server's; the driver suites set `MCM_REQUIRE_BACKUP_TARGETS=1` alongside `MCM_REQUIRE_LIVE_STACK=1` so that a credential- or connectivity-driven skip fails instead of reading as a pass.

Local dev/test infrastructure is four independently operable named Compose projects (auth, mcm, audit, observability) under infrastructure-as-code/docker/stacks/, each a thin include:-only aggregator over that stack's component compose files; the former single root aggregator compose.yaml is retired to a pointer that names the four, and because Compose has no cross-project depends_on the auth stack must be brought up before the mcm app profile (pnpm nx up-auth then pnpm nx up-mcm, or pnpm nx up-all, which serialises auth then mcm).

Within the mcm stack, the no-profile default services are the test infrastructure (mc-service-store-mongo plus its rs-init, mcm-bff-cache-redis, mcm-bff-store-mongo); the app profile adds mc-service, bff-nonsecure and bff-secure add the BFF variants, and agents / agents-metro add the agent layer — and an end-to-end agent flow needs every hop up at once, since movie-mcp calls mc-service with the user's JWT.

mc-service centralizes RBAC rather than checking it per handler: a KeycloakAuthLayer<Role> tower layer plus a require_app_role middleware are applied to the whole protected /api/v1 sub-router, so every business route is protected by default and individual handlers only read claims from KeycloakToken<Role>; /health and /metrics are deliberately merged outside that sub-router and stay unauthenticated.

mc-service's per-collection DAC is enforced through one shared application-layer helper (authorize_collection_access) that every movie command and query calls before reading or writing, so per-collection authorization is uniform and hard to omit; it is deny-by-default and reports a missing collection and an unauthorized caller identically as CollectionNotFound (404) so collection existence does not leak.

The agent-layer Control Tower (LangFuse + OpenTelemetry/Grafana observability, the OpenSearch append-only audit sink, and OPA + Unleash policy/kill-switch) is config-gated and additive: every piece is a no-op with a safe in-code fallback when unconfigured, the observability and policy services are opt-in behind the observability profile, and the audit sink is deployable on its own audit profile — so the app and agent layer run without the Control Tower in dev.

Production shared *infrastructure* secrets — among them the Agent Gateway's Keycloak OAuth client secret (RFC 8693 token exchange) and the BFF master encryption key — are held in Komodo Variables and injected at deploy into each stack's gitignored env file, and no user, model-provider or TMDB credential is ever stored there because those are per-user by design; HashiCorp Vault is deployed in production dormant (uninitialized and sealed) and is not a secret source for any core stack.

Because the BFF's own MongoDB (`mcm-bff-db`) is a standalone instance with no multi-document transactions available, feature 073's exactly-once backup scheduling rests on a single-document atomic claim rather than a transaction, and the Redis leader lock beside it is an optimisation with a TTL guess in it rather than the guarantee.

No Compose stack is profile-gated as a whole: the `auth` and `mcm` stacks each start services with no profile at all, and the per-service `profiles:` assignments live in the included component compose files rather than being re-declared in the stack aggregator (which also removes the include-override merge and lets the stack parse on any conformant Compose).

The BFF's own MongoDB store carries three families of data rather than the per-user agent config alone: the `user_agent_config` collection (per-user encrypted assistant credentials), a single-document global `app_settings` collection, and feature 073's backup state in its own `backup_destinations`, `backup_jobs` and `backup_runs` collections.

Feature 083 puts the scheduled-backup offline-consent round trip on its own Keycloak client, `mcm-backup-consent`, selected by `BACKUP_CONSENT_CLIENT_ID` (with `BACKUP_CONSENT_CLIENT_SECRET` defaulting to the login client's secret), because Keycloak attaches the offline grant to the member's existing SSO session and revoking a grant issued to the LOGIN client therefore ends that member's sign-in session; when the variable is unset the BFF falls back to the login client, and the dedicated client must already exist in the realm because realm imports are `IGNORE_EXISTING`.

The WebDAV backup destination runs on the official Debian `httpd:2.4` image rather than the purpose-built `ghcr.io/hacdias/webdav` Go server it replaced, and not on `httpd:2.4-alpine`: the fail-closed CVE sweep runs on a CI runner with no Docker socket, so Trivy falls back to `remote` and ghcr.io refuses its anonymous token request (`DENIED`), making an unreadable image a red required check rather than a skipped one; and Alpine's `apr-util` ships no DBM driver, so `mod_dav_fs` cannot satisfy the `DavLockDB` that `mod_dav` consults on every write and answers 500.

Bringing the backup destinations up means two long-lived servers plus two one-shot init containers: the S3 init PUTs the test bucket (a driver suite failing on `NoSuchBucket` reads like a driver bug) and the WebDAV init writes the Apache config and a bcrypt `htpasswd` into a named volume rather than a bind mount, because the dev container's Docker is a sandbox microVM that shares only `/workspaces` and would otherwise mount an empty directory. Both one-shots take their credentials from the container's own environment (`$$VAR`) instead of Compose interpolation so the value never lands in the container's argv, and each server carries its own healthcheck — RustFS its `/health/ready`, WebDAV the 401 an unauthenticated request earns, probed over bash `/dev/tcp` since that image ships no curl, wget or nc. CI's bring-up step therefore cannot use `--wait` (it exits 1 for a service that exits 0, which both one-shots do) and instead waits for both servers to report `healthy` and both one-shots to have exit code 0, printing the failing container's logs.

CI brings the feature-073 backup destinations up in their own dedicated `app-e2e-bring-up-backup-destinations` step rather than folding them into the Keycloak bring-up, because the two image pulls pushed that step past its calibrated 300 s ceiling and a slow pull then read as "Keycloak would not start" instead of as itself; the step passes no registry input of any kind, and the web E2E gate forwards `E2E_REQUIRE_BACKUP_TARGETS=1` into the Playwright container so `backups.spec.ts` fails rather than skips when the destinations are absent.

The test-database churn that fed that mongod OOM was removed at the harness, not only at mongod: `common::test_db()` leases a bounded pool slot (`mc_test_s<slot>`, at most 64 slots tracked in the `mc_test_pool.leases` collection) and resets the database on acquire rather than on release, while `cleanup_db` is now a deliberate no-op. Cleaning on acquire is the load-bearing inversion, because a panicking test never reaches its own cleanup; the slot is held for the duration of a test and returned by a thread-local destructor, and a lease whose holder pid has exited is reclaimable immediately.

Every Compose service that mounts a MongoDB `/data/db` volume starts as root (`user: "0:0"`) only to re-own that directory once and then drops to the image's `mongod` user with `setpriv`, so `mongod` itself never runs as root. The wrapper exists because 9.0-ubi9 runs mongod as uid 1000 whereas 8.0.8-ubi9 ran it as 998, so a volume written by the older image is foreign-owned and 9.0 dies at start with `Unable to read the storage engine metadata file ... storage.bson` (FileNotOpen) — measured on a copy of the dev volumes. Removing the wrapper makes the next uid change (or a restore made by a different image) an outage on a populated store; removing the drop leaves mongod running as root. `scripts/__tests__/mongo-data-owner.guard.test.mjs` asserts both halves across the dev and prod compose files and executes the wrapper against stubs, so the assertion is about behaviour rather than spelling.

The RustFS side of the backup-destinations compose file is enforced by a written contract in `scripts/__tests__/object-store-service.guard.test.mjs`: it enumerates the three git-tracked compose files carrying a RustFS server (the backups file plus the dev and prod observability files), asserts it FOUND a server and its init in each so the remaining assertions cannot pass vacuously, and then requires one digest-pinned `rustfs/rustfs` image shared across all three, no `user:` key on any RustFS service (the image runs as its own uid 10001 and a fresh volume inherits `/data` from it, so any other uid dies at startup with `Permission denied`), `RUSTFS_*` credentials with a fail-fast `${VAR:?}` secret and no `MINIO_*` alias, RustFS's own `/health/ready` probe with dependants waiting on `service_healthy`, bucket-init credentials referenced from the container's environment rather than interpolated into argv, stdout logging with the console closed, and — for the backups file specifically — exactly the `127.0.0.1:9100:9000` port published with no `:9001` console port.
